hypothesis: Carrying exact White/Black score totals recursively removes repeated parent score scans while preserving the identical delta-ordering search tree, reducing wall-clock overhead without changing any action.
interpretation: All 83 tests passed before the benchmark. Carried scores were checked against authoritative child score totals, and carried ordering was proven action- and expanded-node-equivalent to delta ordering at tested depths.
The carried implementation preserved exactly the same 882, 2409, and 9349 expanded-node counts as delta ordering at depths 2, 3, and 4.

Removing repeated internal parent-score scans produced only a modest additional runtime gain: about 1.6 percent at depth 2, 0.4 percent at depth 3, and 0.9 percent at depth 4 relative to delta ordering.

At depth 3 the engine still reduced expanded nodes by 36.2 percent but remained 58.0 percent slower than Baseline A. At depth 4 it reduced nodes by 44.0 percent but remained 11.7 percent slower than Baseline A.

This result localizes the remaining move-ordering overhead further: repeated score scans are not the dominant cost. Child-state construction, action generation, sorting, and the unchanged leaf evaluator now account for most of the remaining gap.

The Stage 2 evidence no longer supports chasing additional micro-optimizations of the same score-ordering estimate without a new hypothesis. Structural exact TT is already a wall-clock win at depth 4 on its own, while ordering provides much larger node reductions but remains runtime-negative in Python.
A sensible next Stage 2 decision point is therefore to compare production-relevant search configurations under a fixed time budget rather than continue optimizing fixed-depth traversal in isolation.
